paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So when we think about the word tartuk [MTHAR THUG] — thinking about rejoicing — what are we really rejoicing in? Because this is a V Houses class. For all of you teachers out there, we should mention the ancient texts. Where does this come from?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: The simple way of discussing the four steps — let's call it level one. Is, what do you want? So then, you decide what you want. There's nothing wrong with what I'm saying right now. You should do all of these things. Decide what you want — this is called the basis. Secondly, you make a plan. What’s the word? For a 20 pesos. The word for making a plan, in Tibetan.

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: Sampa.
{Tim gives money to two people}

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Sam-pa [BSAM PA]. It's the planning period, right? So if I want more money, I'm like, I've got to help somebody. So what am I going to do? I'm going to bring some money from the United States, I'm going to go to the exchange, and I'm going to get some Mexican pesos. And I'm going to give that money out during the class. I made that plan yesterday. I put the money in my bag. So then I acted on it, right? The third step is then acting.

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: Jorwa.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Jorwa [SBYOR BA]. He wants 20 more. Alright. {gives the money}

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So you do it. I went to the exchange place. Me dieron una promoción.

paragraphs.speaker: Interpreter
paragraphs.text: They gave me a promotion.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I was like, that's not a discount, you're still ripping me off. "Well, if you give us $200 more, we'll give you a better rate." Yeah, but I don't buy it anyway. No, I was actually very happy. I was enjoying it. I was like, all right, you can have that extra money, you're going to do something cool with it.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: All right, so, fourth step — which the center is named after. And normally we say that's about rejoicing in your good seeds. When you go to bed at night — and I'm going to do it tonight — I'm going to rejoice in my seed-planting that I did today during class. And then I'm going to just let that seed germinate, and somehow the money will show up again in the future. Great. Keep doing it.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: But what does tartuk really mean? What's the deeper meaning? Remember the whole thing about me — everything that's me right now, the cascade of seeds opening up that go "me." When you tartuk, when you rejoice, you are owning the seed. You are saying, that's me. That's the solution.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: When a seed ripens, it's not like it's you, and then the money that's out there. We'd like to think that way, because it's helpful to think that way. Because it's like, oh look, I got all this money. Or I got praise. Or I got a hot date.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: But understand this deep point about seeds ripening. When the seed ripens, it is ripening as both you and the thing that you're perceiving. It's the same seed. That seed, for when someone gives you money — that seed is opening as both you and the money that's coming at you. So you and the money that's coming back are intricately linked. You're stuck together. And everything you see in the world is like that.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So when you're rejoicing in a seed, you're rejoicing in you. You are that seed. You are the ripening of that seed, excuse me. And everything that's happening in your world is — it's not like it's you and everything else.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Remember how I started with how we're co-creating this tonight? I have my seeds, you have your seeds. Not a problem. But everything that I perceive is coming from me. Whatever is coming from you is coming from you.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: But if I'm offering money out, and then I go home and rejoice, I'm creating a different me. Or I’m creating the limited being that I think I am, and that I’m never going to change from. Lying at night thinking about how nobody loves me. Everything is always going to be like this, it's always terrible. What are you doing? You're saying, that's me. And you're tartukeando that seed. What do you think is going to come out? It's just going to keep coming out that way.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So if we can learn to identify what those things are about ourselves that are just the flow of limited ideas about ourselves and the world — and we stop the tartuking of those ideas, of those me's that I don't want anymore.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: This is why it's entirely useless to complain about other people's failures, or the way that they've treated you wrongly. Because what are you doing? Just putting it back in the ground. It doesn't mean don't have an emotion. It doesn't mean don't talk about it. I didn't say that. It's helpful to understand. But can you catch yourself so that you don't do this? And how do you develop that awareness so that you stop planting the you's that you don't want anymore?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Change you, change the world. If you're having problems with money, you need to look at your belief system of who you think you are. And then you know what seeds to plant. It's not enough to say, oh, I have this limiting belief about myself.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: That was really kind, by the way. That was super kind, that she went and got her water. That was really cool, thank you.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Teaching moment. What did I just do?

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: Rejoiced? You make us realize that we have to be more kind.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Yes, but there's a technique to it. You all are already very, very kind people. You're already good people. You wouldn't be in this room if you weren't. But how do we accelerate? How do we activate? So I want to go back — what did I just do in this moment when I saw the water being offered to the person who's having a cough?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: First, someone said, I noticed it. I paid attention to it. I called it out. I even said, wow, that's really cool. And I was really happy about that. Why? Because I want those things in my world. I want to see more of them. I don't want to see more negativity. There's enough of it. I could start making a list right now. But if I continue down that track and make a list of all this stuff that bothers me, and I tartuk [MTHAR THUG] about it — this is why I'm saying, yes, you can talk about things that bother you, but there's a difference between tartuking about it and then trying to change it. So I want more of that in my world, so I'm going to point it out and I'm going to celebrate it.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Okay, and now I have one more point on that, and then we'll explore it more tomorrow. Why did I see Ari get up and go get water and help Rosalia because she needed some water when she was coughing? I have the seed. Another way of saying that is: in the past, I was kind before. I did something before. My past self created future self. And what do I want my future self to be? I want more of that. So I'm taking care of future Tim.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And I'm not focusing on the negative, because it was interesting — when she got up and left, I was like, I wonder if I'm boring. Seriously. I was like, I wonder if I did something wrong. Did I say something wrong? And then when she came back with the water, I was like — watch what your mind does. “I was boring.” That Tim came forward. Do I want to keep on thinking that I'm boring? But I didn't. I had no control of it in the moment. And then the seed changed. Thank God it didn't continue to cascade that way.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: How many times do you do the same thing? You assume what's going on, and it's about you. How egotistical is it of me to think she's bored in the class that I'm teaching? And we are doing this all the time. And if she had just left — I mean, there's a million reasons. Maybe she got a phone call. Maybe she has to go home. There's a billion reasons that have nothing to do with me. And that is 99.999% of your world. It has nothing to do with you. Even thinking about you. The funniest thing of it is — like, I'm worried about being bored. Let's say I'm on a date with somebody. I'm so self-conscious about myself. Does this person like me? My hotness. That person's not even thinking, is he nice, is he hot? That person's thinking, am I hot enough? We're both having an insane conversation to ourselves.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So what stories about yourself do you want to create? And so this practice is a practice of storytelling. Start listening to your stories. "I am. It is always like this. It'll never change. Me, me, me, me, me." And it's funny, but it's the truth. And then when you can bring awareness to those stories, then you have a potential to change that. And it's not an affirmation. It's the four steps, right?
